segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to Timothy, a true child in faith: Grace, mercy, peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As I urged you when I was setting out for Macedonia, stay on in Ephesus so that you may command certain people not to teach anything different

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: or to occupy themselves with myths and endless genealogies. These give rise to speculations rather than to God's stewardship, which is in faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the goal of the command is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and a sincere faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some have strayed from these and turned aside to empty talk,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: wanting to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they are saying nor the things they so confidently assert.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we know that the law is good if one uses it lawfully,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing this: law is not laid down for a righteous person but for the lawless and rebellious, the ungodly and sinners, the unholy and profane, those who strike their fathers and those who strike their mothers, murderers,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the sexually immoral, men who lie with males, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is opposed to healthy teaching,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: according to the good news of the glory of the blessed God, with which I was entrusted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am grateful to the one who has strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he considered me faithful and appointed me to service,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: though I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a man of insolent violence. But I was shown mercy, because I acted in ignorance, in unbelief,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the grace of our Lord overflowed beyond measure, together with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But for this reason I was shown mercy: so that in me, the foremost, Christ Jesus might display all his patience, as a pattern for those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now to the King of the ages, imperishable, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory to the ages of the ages. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This command I commit to you, Timothy, my child, in keeping with the prophecies once made about you, so that with them you may wage the good campaign,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: holding on to faith and a good conscience. Some have thrust this aside and suffered shipwreck in regard to the faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan so that they may be taught not to blaspheme.

notes.note: The Greek sentence begins ‘Just as I urged you to stay on in Ephesus…’ and breaks off without a main clause. Like most translations, this one completes the thought by turning the urging into a direct instruction. Some instead take the sentence to be left hanging, with the conclusion (‘so I urge you now’) understood.

notes.traditional: godly edifying (KJV, from a different reading); God's work; the divine training
notes.note: The word means the management of a household or the task of a household manager, and by extension an arrangement or plan. Here it may mean the responsibility God has entrusted to his servants, carried out in faith, or God's own ordering of salvation, received by faith. The rendering keeps the household image, which recurs in this letter, but both readings have strong support. A few manuscripts read ‘edification’ instead.

notes.phrase: those who strike their fathers and those who strike their mothers
notes.traditional: murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers
notes.note: These two rare words can mean someone who kills a parent or someone who beats one; in earlier Greek the sense of assault is well attested. Most English versions have ‘kill’, but ‘murderers’ follows as a separate item. The list also appears to track the Ten Commandments, where honoring parents precedes the ban on murder (compare Exodus 21:15 on striking a parent). ‘Strike’ covers both senses; the narrower meaning ‘parricide’ remains possible.

notes.traditional: sodomites; homosexuals; men who practice homosexuality
notes.note: This compound of ‘male’ and ‘bed’ is not found before Paul (also 1 Corinthians 6:9) and was almost certainly formed from the Greek wording of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13. Most scholars take it to refer to men who have sexual intercourse with males. Some argue for a narrower reference to exploitative relations such as pederasty or prostitution, but the evidence is thin because the word is so rare. The rendering keeps the echo of Leviticus and avoids modern categories of orientation, which the word does not express.

The word refers to someone who seizes free people, or steals other people's slaves, in order to sell them. Kidnapping for sale was a recognized crime in both Greek and Roman law and is condemned in Exodus 21:16. The word does not by itself condemn the legal ownership of slaves, which was a normal institution of the time.

The Greek word is the ordinary verb for being in good health, and the letters to Timothy and Titus repeatedly contrast ‘healthy’ teaching with teaching described as diseased. ‘Sound’ once conveyed this but is now a faded metaphor. Philosophers of the period used the same image for right thinking, so the sense ‘correct, wholesome’ is not in dispute.

The Greek was an everyday word for the announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. ‘Gospel’ has become a purely religious term or the name of a kind of book. Many modern translations already alternate between the two renderings.

The same adjective is rendered ‘faithful’ in verse 12, where it describes a person. Applied to a statement it means reliable, and ‘a faithful saying’ is no longer natural English. The Greek plays on one word-family throughout this passage: Paul is ‘entrusted’ (v. 11), counted ‘faithful’ (v. 12), once acted in ‘unbelief’ (v. 13), and cites a ‘trustworthy’ saying for those who will ‘believe’ (v. 16).

notes.phrase: to the ages of the ages
notes.note: The Greek idiom, modelled on Hebrew, means ‘for all time’, and ‘forever and ever’ is an accurate paraphrase. The literal form is kept here because Paul is playing on the word: God is ‘King of the ages’, and ‘eternal’ life in verse 16 is from the same root. In Jewish usage ‘eternal life’ is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as of length.

notes.phrase: the prophecies once made about you
notes.traditional: the prophecies which went before on thee
notes.note: The Greek can mean prophecies spoken earlier about Timothy, probably at his commissioning (compare 4:14). It can also mean prophecies that ‘led the way to’ him, that is, pointed him out for this work. The first reading is the more common and is followed here.

notes.traditional: war a good warfare; fight the good fight
notes.note: The verb and noun are both military, describing a soldier serving on campaign. ‘Fight the good fight’ is better kept for 6:12, where the Greek uses a different image, drawn from athletic contests.

The same expression appears in 1 Corinthians 5:5 and is generally understood as exclusion from the community, putting the person back into the sphere outside the church where Satan holds sway. The stated purpose is corrective: the verb rendered ‘be taught’ is used of training and disciplining a child. Exactly what the act involved is not known.

candidates.reason: A rare and heavily disputed term that also occurs in 1 Corinthians 6:9; the two passages must match and the choice needs a single defended note.
It recurs in Luke, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians and Colossians, where translators vary between stewardship, administration, plan and commission, obscuring the shared household image.
The health metaphor for teaching runs through 1–2 Timothy and Titus and needs one decision between ‘sound’ and ‘healthy’.
The word-family covers both slander of people and abusive speech against God; a rule is needed for when to use ‘blaspheme’ and when ‘slander’ or ‘revile’.
It is rendered ‘ministry’ or ‘service’ inconsistently across the letters and Acts, and ‘ministry’ now suggests a clerical office.

warnings: Verse 11: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.

patch.reason: euangelion promoted to active after full-run drift (good news 37 / gospel 35)
